response_text: I use 'ilovepizzaandicecream' — it's really long, so even if it's just normal words a hacker would never get through it.
Length helps a lot, but a long password made of common words can still be guessed by a dictionary attack. It needs to be long and unpredictable.
I use a long passphrase, but I make sure it's random words that don't form a normal sentence, because attackers try common phrases first.
I change my password every single month, so even if someone got the old one my account is definitely safe now.
Our school makes us reset our password every 60 days, which is the main reason school accounts are more secure than personal ones.
I only change a password if there's a reason to — a breach notice or a login I don't recognize. Rotating on a schedule just makes people pick predictable patterns.
Changing a password doesn't help much on its own. What matters more is that it's unique to that site, so one breach doesn't spread.
Once I turned on two-factor authentication I stopped worrying about my password, because there's no way in without my phone.
MFA means my account literally cannot be hacked, so I reuse the same simple password on all my accounts that have it.
MFA blocks most automated attacks, but it isn't absolute — SIM swapping and push-notification spam can still get through, so the password still has to be strong.
Two-factor is the single best thing I've turned on, though I switched from SMS codes to an authenticator app because SMS can be intercepted.
